messages.subject: 2.4+ manual and ease of finding things
parts:
The 2.3 manual isn't going to make things easier to find.

In fact, it splits out the CmdStan part, which will arguably
make things harder to find.

Michael drafted a new manual outline that'll hopefully make
things easier. Andrew and I have also been discussing some re-orgs.

But this particular issue, support matching constraints, is
emphasized right up front in the CmdStan manual.

The hard-to-find problem is intrinsic to large systems because
you can't emphasize everything. We could add an index,
but I don't think it'll help with this kind of thing, because
it's an unknown unknown for a user and they won't know what
to look up.

- Bob

>>> On Wednesday, June 11, 2014 1:11:38 PM UTC-4, Hang Zeng wrote:
>>> My model compiles good and can run. But it is very slow and it always get like this "Iteration: 1/10000 [ 0%] (warmup)".
>>> I get the initial values from in2extRemes package which are reasonable. I stop the running and check the results which reveals that the first several iterations are near to initial values and then change so much. Here is my simple model. Can someone help with that? Thank you!
>>>
>>> For distributions like the GEV where the support depends on the parameter values, you have to be clever with the declarations in the parameters section. Otherwise, you get into a situation where what Stan thinks are valid parameter values have zero or undefined density values. In your case, it would be something like
>>>
>>> data {
>>> int<lower=0> n; vector[n] t; real y[n];}
>>> transformed data {
>>> real min_y;
>>> real max_y;
>>> min_y <- min(y);
>>> max_y <- max(y);
>>> }
>>> parameters {
>>> real xi;
>>> real<lower=0> sigma;
>>> real<lower=if_else( xi > 0, min_y + sigma / xi, negative_infinity() ),
>>> upper=if_else( xi > 0, infinity(), max_y + sigma / xi )> mu;
>>> }
>>> model {
>>> real z;
>>> for(i in 1:n) {
>>> z <- 1 + (y[i] - mu) * xi / sigma;
>>> increment_log_prob(-log(sigma) - (1 + 1/xi)*log(z[n]) - pow(z,-1/xi));
>>> }
>>> // priors on xi, sigma, and mu
>>> }
>>>
>>> Ben
